voicevox.intro: <slot0/> converts the AudioQuery used by VOICEVOX synthesis into a LipSyncTrack. Shared dialogue components, WAV-based lip sync, and LipSyncTrack remain in <slot1/>. Import the adapter from its own package; it is no longer re-exported from @celesta/react.
voicevox.runtime: The desktop app and CLI bundle this package separately. Building @celesta/react builds it too, and File → Set Up TypeScript includes its declarations and import mapping. It is private and is not published to npm. The browser playground does not support it.
voicevox.example: Drive a dialogue line from its synthesis query
voicevox.query: Use the exact AudioQuery that produced the WAV, including speed and pause settings. Pass the track to Dialogue or CharacterView as lipSync, or read it with useLipSync(). It does not synthesize audio or call a VOICEVOX server. Save that AudioQuery as voicevox-query.json beside voicevox.tsx, and use your own voice and mouth images in the example below.

api.voicevox-convert: Convert an AudioQuery into a LipSyncTrack, with time zero at the start of the WAV, including leading silence.
api.voicevox-vowel: Map a phoneme to a/i/u/e/o/closed. Uppercase devoiced vowels keep their shape; N, cl, pau, sil, and unknown values map to closed.
api.voicevox-frame-rate: Defaults to 93.75 Hz, the VOICEVOX phoneme frame grid. Set null for unrounded lengths or the engine’s own rate; this is not the composition’s fps.
api.voicevox-upspeak: Defaults to true. Set false when the WAV was synthesized with interrogative upspeak disabled.

voicevox.types: Exports also include VoicevoxAudioQuery, VoicevoxAccentPhrase, VoicevoxMora, and VoicevoxLipSyncOptions. LipSyncTrack is imported from @celesta/react.

The exporter then prints no progress, only one line of JSON when it finishes: the status, every file it wrote, warnings, the composition's size, fps and frame count once the exporter has loaded it, and on failure an error code and message. shared.encoding-options-body: MP4 uses libx264 with --preset medium and --crf 18 by default. Faster presets such as veryfast reduce encoding time but usually increase file size at similar quality. CRF accepts 0–51; lower values give higher quality and larger files. --color-conversion accepts auto, gpu, or encoder. --render-quality draft speeds up timing checks by skipping scaled-text re-rasterization; use final (the default) to judge the finished image.
shared.export-a-draft: Export with a faster encoder preset
shared.png-frames-body: --frame / --frames selects zero-based frame numbers. Multiple frames create names such as check-000090.png. --every N selects every Nth frame of the --from/--to range (or the whole composition) and its last frame. Add --contact-sheet to place them in one labelled grid; --columns and --tile-width control its layout. Explicit frame numbers cannot be combined with --every, --from, or --to.
shared.graphics-driver-body: Both the editor and exporter accept --driver auto (default), vulkan, dx12 (Windows), metal (macOS), or gl. Auto chooses an available adapter in wgpu’s backend order: Vulkan, Metal, DX12, then OpenGL. A specific driver must be available in the build and supported by the machine. This chooses the rendering API; MP4 encoding still uses libx264.
shared.audio-frame-keyframes: frameKeyframes(keys, { fps, origin? }) builds volume or playbackRate keyframes from frame numbers. Times are (frame - origin) / fps on the enclosing sequence’s clock; origin defaults to 0. Use it for audio fades. The browser exporter only supports constant volume and playback rate.
